title: A vorticity map is only honest on a fixed, symmetric colour scale, and it needs a number beside it
summary: Colour maps of vorticity, filtered fields, difference fields and their videos show where the structures are. They cannot say how much energy they hold or how fast it decays, so every such figure must be read with its colour limits and paired with a spectrum or a time history.

media.alt: Three square vorticity maps on a 0 to 6.3 domain with one shared red-blue colour bar from about minus 70 to plus 70. Left: random initial condition, pale and fine-grained. Centre: coarse grid, no model, t = 1, with stronger small blue and red cells. Right: coarse grid with a Smagorinsky model, t = 1, paler and smoother than the centre.

read_the_figure.question: How does the vorticity field of the same initial condition differ on a coarse grid with and without a sub-grid model, and what changes between the left, centre and right panels?
read_the_figure.axes: x and y: position in a doubly periodic square of side about 6.3 (2 pi). Colour: vorticity (red: counter-clockwise rotation, blue: clockwise), one diverging colour bar shared by the three panels, symmetric about zero.
look_at: Check the colour bar first. It is shared and symmetric, so the same colour means the same vorticity in every panel. That is what makes the panels comparable.

Left to centre: the field keeps its pattern but strong small cells appear (look at the dark blue cell near x = 4, y = 3.2). Without a model, the grid scale holds more rotation than the initial field had at that scale.
Centre to right: the model panel is paler overall. A sub-grid eddy viscosity removes small-scale vorticity, and it also lowers the overall amplitude. Pale means less vorticity, not 'cleaner flow'.
In the video posters, read the title time and the colour limits. Different panels of the group use different limits (about 20, 30, 70 in the posters), so do not compare colour across figures.
Notice that the field is never a pure picture of 'where the vortices are': two nearby cells of opposite sign can hide a strong shear layer between them.
read_the_figure.proves: Side by side on one fixed colour scale, the panels show that the unmodelled coarse run develops more small-scale structure than the modelled one. Pictures alone do not quantify the difference: pair them with the spectrum of the energy-spectrum explainer.
if_wrong: Colour limits that change from frame to frame (autoscale): a decaying field then looks as if it never weakens. A fixed scale is the first thing to check in any animation.
A non-symmetric limit on a diverging map: zero is no longer white, and positive and negative vorticity cannot be compared.

Interpolated pixels (smooth bicubic) in one figure and nearest-cell squares in another: the same data look different. The filmstrip of the instrument panel is drawn in squares and its poster is smoothed.
A band-pass or difference field presented on the same scale as the full field: a small signal then looks absent. Rescale and say so.
must_check: The colour bar: limits stated, symmetric about zero, identical across the panels that are compared.
The time or frame label on every panel and whether the animation has a fixed scale.
Resolution (cells) and the model coefficient in the caption.
That the picture is paired with a number: a spectrum, an energy history or a norm.
For a difference panel, that it is zero at t = 0 and that its colour scale is stated (in the divergence figure it is grey, i.e. zero, in the first frame).
as_drawn: Values read by eye, about 20 percent.
The shared colour bar of the snapshot figure spans about minus 70 to plus 70; the initial field uses only the pale middle of it (peaks near plus or minus 30).
Instrument-panel poster, bottom right: energy over its initial value falls to about 0.69 and enstrophy over its initial value to about 0.22 at t = 2.5.
Closure-divergence poster: the running L2 difference between the two models rises from 0 to about 7.7 over t = 0 to 2; its units are not normalised in the figure.
Pipeline poster: vorticity limits about plus or minus 30; the pipeline demo figure shows gradient magnitudes up to about 140.

terms.meaning: The local rotation of the fluid. In 2D it is one number per point: the curl of the velocity.
A map with a neutral centre (white) for zero and two hues for positive and negative values. It needs symmetric limits.
The same colour limits for every frame of an animation. Without it the eye cannot see decay.
The sub-grid model that adds a viscosity proportional to the strain rate and to the square of the filter width.
Keeps only wavenumbers between two limits. The sum of all bands is the original field.
Net energy transfer from small to large scales. A local eddy-viscosity model cannot produce it by construction, since its dissipation is never negative.
Quantising the field by the integer part of log10 of its magnitude, so each colour is one order of magnitude.
A contour line connects points of equal value (here omega = 0, where vorticity changes sign). A gradient filter computes the slope of the field by differences between neighbours.
A still taken from a video (first frame) and a row of frames at chosen times: static summaries of a time series.

remember: A colour map shows the pattern, not the amount. Always keep the colour bar and a quantitative companion.
In a periodic 2D flow without forcing, energy and enstrophy both decay; enstrophy decays faster, so the typical scale grows.
An eddy-viscosity model only removes energy at the resolved scales. It never adds any.
Fixed, symmetric colour limits make frames and panels comparable.
A band-pass series partitions energy: the band energies add up to the total (Parseval).
A difference field is zero at the start if the initial conditions are identical; growth from zero is the divergence.

understand.title: The same data, many encodings
understand.text: The group is one decaying vorticity field drawn in different ways: raw colour (snapshots and the evolution video), colour plus spectrum plus history (instrument panel), colour by scale (telescope), colour by sign of energy transfer (backscatter map), colour by order of magnitude (decade bands), derived fields (contour and gradient), and two models side by side with their difference. Each encoding answers one question and hides others. A decade-band map, for instance, makes the thin lines where vorticity changes sign visible as dark threads, but it flattens everything above its top band into one colour.

understand.title: Reading a video as a figure
understand.text: A video adds time but removes the possibility of comparing two instants side by side. The honest way to read it is to pause on a few frames, as the filmstrip does, and to read the companion curves. The instrument panel is designed for this: the energy and enstrophy history shows what the pictures cannot.

understand.title: Reading a derived field
understand.text: A contour of omega = 0 is the boundary between clockwise and counter-clockwise regions. The gradient magnitude highlights thin shear layers. Both are computed on a coarse grid with differences between neighbours, so on this resolution they inherit the pixel structure and their accuracy is limited by the grid spacing.

steps.title: The vorticity equation of 2D flow
steps.note: There is no vortex stretching in 2D, so vorticity is carried along by the flow and only diffused by viscosity. That is why vortices of the same sign can merge but small ones cannot be created by stretching. With a model, nu is replaced by nu plus the eddy viscosity.

steps.title: Energy and enstrophy decay
steps.note: Averages over a periodic box. Both rates are negative. Since P is large when there is fine structure, enstrophy is destroyed much faster than energy, which is what the instrument-panel history shows.

steps.title: A mean wavenumber from the two histories
steps.note: The ratio of the two normalised curves gives the typical wavenumber of the flow. If enstrophy falls faster than energy, k_m falls: the energy-containing scale grows. This is the quantitative content of 'vortices merge'.

steps.title: What the Smagorinsky model does to the field
steps.note: The model dissipation is never negative, so it can only drain resolved energy. With a filter width of one grid cell on a 32-point grid of side 2 pi (width 0.196) and a coefficient 0.17, (C_s Delta)^2 is about 1.1e-3, so a strain rate of 10 gives an eddy viscosity of about 0.011, some twenty times the molecular value 5e-4 of the energy-spectrum case. That explains why the modelled panel is much paler.

steps.title: Band-pass partitions the energy
steps.note: Non-overlapping windows in k are orthogonal, so the energy of the bands adds up. The telescope sweeps 12 such windows. Low-k windows show a few broad blobs (k below 2.8 in the poster), high-k windows show thin filaments.

steps.title: Backscatter is a sign of the flux
steps.note: The backscatter map keeps only the wavenumber shells where the resolved-scale flux is negative at that instant and displays the field those shells hold. It is not the same as the sub-grid dissipation, which is never negative for an eddy-viscosity model.

steps.title: A centred difference and its error
steps.note: The gradient filter uses differences of this type, so its error scales with the square of the grid spacing and is largest at the thinnest layers, exactly where the gradient magnitude peaks. The same Taylor argument as in the convergence explainer.

steps.title: A decade band
steps.note: Wherever omega changes sign it passes through zero, so every sign boundary is a thread of very small magnitude. If the top band is clipped, all values above its lower edge share one colour, which hides the dynamic range.

worked.title: How much did the typical scale grow?
worked.problem: At t = 2.5 the instrument-panel history shows energy at 0.69 and enstrophy at 0.22 of their initial values. By what factor has the mean wavenumber changed?

solution.text: Use the ratio of normalised histories.

worked.answer: The mean wavenumber has fallen to about 0.56 of its initial value, so the typical length scale has grown by about 1.8 times.

analyze.q: In the snapshot figure the modelled panel is paler than the unmodelled one. Is that more evidence that the model is 'good'? What measurement would tell you whether the amount of removal is right?
analyze.hint: A reference spectrum from a finer run or a DNS.

analyze.q: The decade-band map has most cells in the top band. If the top band is clipped at its lower edge, what would the caption's claim 'most of the domain sits at decade 0' actually mean?
analyze.hint: Compare with the vorticity ranges of other figures (plus or minus 15 or more) and the colour bar's top tick.

analyze.q: Two animation frames look equally colourful although the energy has dropped by half. Which plotting choice could cause it?

evaluate.q: The closure-divergence figure shows a growing L2 difference. What does it prove, and what does it not tell you about which model is closer to the truth?
evaluate.hint: There is no reference field in that figure.

evaluate.q: Is a movie a good primary evidence for a modelling claim? When is a filmstrip better?
evaluate.hint: Time comparison, pausing and the need for a number.

create: Draw a six-frame filmstrip with one fixed symmetric colour bar and a strip under it with energy and enstrophy ratios with a cursor, so a reader of the PDF gets the same information as the video.
Design a decade-band map whose lowest and highest bands are open-ended (below and above) and labelled as such.

checks.q: Why does a diverging colour map need symmetric limits?
checks.answer: Because the neutral colour (white) must stand for zero. With asymmetric limits, zero shifts to a tint, positive and negative values of the same size get different colours, and the eye misreads the sign balance.

checks.q: Energy falls to 0.50 and enstrophy to 0.20 of their initial values. By how much has the mean wavenumber changed?
checks.hint: Square root of the ratio of the two histories.
checks.answer: sqrt(0.20 / 0.50) = sqrt(0.4), about 0.63 of its initial value.

checks.q: Why can an eddy-viscosity model not produce backscatter?
checks.hint: What is the sign of nu_t times the squared strain rate?
checks.answer: Its dissipation is nu_t |S|^2 with nu_t >= 0, which is never negative. The model can only remove resolved energy; energy moving up-scale must come from the resolved flux, which the backscatter map shows from the resolved field, not from the model.

checks.q: A video shows a field that looks the same at the start and the end. What do you check before concluding that nothing decayed?
checks.answer: Whether the colour limits are fixed across frames. If the scale rescales each frame, the picture stays equally vivid even when the amplitude has fallen. Also look at the companion energy curve if there is one.

checks.q: How would you quantify the difference between the modelled and unmodelled snapshot panels in one number?
checks.hint: A normalised norm of a difference against a reference.
checks.answer: Take a reference field (a finer run filtered to the coarse grid) and compute the relative L2 difference of each coarse field to it, or compare their spectra band by band. The model is better where that number is smaller.
